lead: Concrete cracks when the tensile stress at its extreme fibre reaches a small fraction of its compressive strength. Before that point the beam is uncracked and behaves elastically. The modular ratio m lets you replace steel bars by an equivalent area of concrete, so one neutral axis and one second moment of area give the stresses. The same transformed section gives the cracking moment Mcr, the bending moment at which the first flexural crack appears. Deflection checks, crack initiation and the switch to a cracked-section analysis all use Mcr.
prereq: You need: concrete properties and limit state philosophy (see Unit 1, Design Philosophies and Material Behaviour) and the singly reinforced beam neutral-axis idea in Chapter 2.1.

blocks.text: At loads below Mcr the beam is uncracked and behaves elastically. Plane sections stay plane, so concrete and steel at the same level have the same strain. Stress is E times strain. Steel has Es = 200,000 N/mm²; concrete has Ec = 5000√fck N/mm², where fck is characteristic cube strength in N/mm². The modular ratio is m = Es/Ec. For M25, fck = 25 N/mm², Ec = 25,000 N/mm², m = 8.00. Steel stress is m times the concrete stress at the same level. The value of m is short-term; creep under sustained load raises the effective m. This chapter uses the short-term value. The transformed section replaces steel by an equivalent concrete area so that one elastic analysis gives both materials' stresses. Cracking moment uses this uncracked section, not the cracked section of Chapter 2.6. Under normal service loads a reinforced beam is already cracked; the uncracked transformed section gives Mcr, not the service stresses. A small tensile stress can crack concrete even when the steel is nowhere near yield.

sections.h3: Transformed section for an uncracked beam

blocks.text: Steel displaces concrete. In the uncracked section, tension steel of area Ast sits at effective depth d. Replace it by (m−1)Ast of concrete at the same level. The mAst supplies the steel force; the −Ast removes the concrete that is not there. Use (m−1)Ast, not mAst. For b width, D overall depth and ybar from the compression face:

blocks.where: ybar is distance from compression face in mm; b is width in mm; D is overall depth in mm; d is effective depth in mm; Ast is tension steel area in mm²; m is modular ratio.

blocks.text: The second moment about the neutral axis is

blocks.where: I is second moment of area about the neutral axis in mm⁴; other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: Here b and D are in mm, Ast in mm², d and ybar in mm, and I in mm⁴. Concrete stress at distance y from the neutral axis is σc = M y / I, where M is bending moment in N·mm. Steel stress before cracking is σs = m M (d−ybar)/I. After cracking, concrete tension is ignored; the cracked transformed section uses mAst and a new neutral axis. That section gives steel stress after cracking. It is not used for Mcr.

The first flexural crack forms when the tensile stress at the extreme tension fibre reaches the flexural tensile strength fr = 0.7√fck N/mm². This is a mean value, not a design strength. The cracking moment is Mcr = fr I / yt. I and ybar come from the uncracked transformed section. yt is the distance from the neutral axis to the extreme tension fibre; for a bottom-tension beam yt = D − ybar. With fr in N/mm², I in mm⁴ and yt in mm, Mcr is in N·mm; divide by 10⁶ for kN·m. Use Mcr to decide whether a service moment causes cracking. If Mservice > Mcr, use the cracked section for deflection and steel stress, as in Chapter 2.6. If Mservice ≤ Mcr, the section is uncracked and the transformed uncracked section applies. Mcr is not the ultimate moment and must not be compared directly with a factored design moment.

blocks.where: Mcr is cracking moment in N·mm; fr = 0.7√fck is flexural tensile strength in N/mm²; I is uncracked transformed second moment of area in mm⁴; yt is distance from neutral axis to extreme tension fibre in mm.

examples.question: A rectangular beam has b = 300 mm, D = 500 mm, d = 450 mm, Ast = 1200 mm² and fck = 25 N/mm². Take Es = 200,000 N/mm² and Ec = 5000√fck. Find the modular ratio m and the uncracked transformed-section cracking moment Mcr.
steps: Gross concrete area Ac = bD = 300 × 500 = 150,000 mm². Its centroid is D/2 = 250 mm from the compression face.
Net transformed steel area As' = (m − 1)Ast = (8 − 1) × 1200 = 8400 mm² at d = 450 mm.

traps: Using mAst instead of (m − 1)Ast for tension steel in an uncracked transformed section. The −Ast removes concrete displaced by the bar.
Using the cracked transformed-section I to compute Mcr. Mcr belongs to the uncracked section; the cracked section is for post-cracking steel stress.
Taking yt as D/2 or D. Find the neutral axis of the transformed section first; for bottom tension yt = D − ybar.
Forgetting units: fr in N/mm², I in mm⁴, yt in mm give Mcr in N·mm. Divide by 10⁶ for kN·m.
Treating fr = 0.7√fck as a design strength and comparing Mcr directly with factored Mu. Mcr is a mean cracking value, not a limit-state strength.

quiz.q: Define modular ratio m and state Es.
quiz.a: m = Es/Ec is the ratio of steel to concrete elastic moduli in the uncracked elastic range. For reinforcing steel Es = 200,000 N/mm².

quiz.q: Why is tension steel replaced by (m − 1)Ast, not mAst, in an uncracked transformed section?
quiz.a: Steel occupies an area Ast where concrete is absent. mAst gives the concrete area equivalent to the steel force, but the missing concrete Ast must be subtracted. Net addition = mAst − Ast = (m − 1)Ast.

quiz.q: For fck = 30 N/mm², find Ec and m. Use Es = 200,000 N/mm².
A beam's fck is increased while b, D, d and Ast stay fixed. Explain the effect on Ec, m and the uncracked neutral axis.
quiz.a: Ec increases, so m decreases. The transformed steel area (m − 1)Ast decreases, so the neutral axis moves slightly back toward mid-depth. The change is small because the steel area is a small part of the section.

quiz.q: Write the expression for flexural tensile strength fr and give its units.
quiz.a: fr = 0.7√fck, with fck in N/mm², so fr is in N/mm².

quiz.q: Why can the cracked transformed section not be used to calculate Mcr?
quiz.a: Mcr is the moment at first crack, before tension concrete is lost. The cracked section already assumes zero concrete tension and uses mAst, with a different neutral axis and I. Using that I in fr I / yt gives the wrong cracking moment.

quiz.q: Ignoring steel, a gross section gives Mcr = 43.75 kN·m for the worked example. Explain why the transformed section gives 50.34 kN·m.
quiz.a: The transformed steel area adds stiffness at depth d, moves the neutral axis downward toward the steel and changes yt. In the example I rises and yt falls, so fr I / yt rises. The gross section underestimates Mcr; it is a conservative simplification.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software for non-linear section analysis uses the same transformed-section idea but updates m and the cracked tension zone as loading rises. Tension stiffening between cracks is modelled with an effective moment of inertia; search for tension stiffening and effective moment of inertia. Code-based crack-width checks use bond and cover, not Mcr alone. Creep and shrinkage change the effective modular ratio, so long-term transformed sections use an age-adjusted Ec. Search for age-adjusted modular ratio and transformed section creep.
